Fixes g-reviewer:29 (high): gitrepo::run shelled out via Command::output with no deadline, so a stalled or lock-starved remote transport (fetch/push/ls-remote) blocked it forever -- and since almost every bus command starts with fetch_remote, one stuck transport hung inbox, status, review take, audit-main, and everything else behind it with no diagnostic. Every git invocation now goes through run_command_with_timeout: spawn with piped stdout/stderr drained on background threads (to avoid a full pipe buffer deadlocking the wait), poll try_wait with exponential backoff capped at 50ms against a 30s deadline, and on expiry kill the whole process tree rather than just the immediate git process -- git spawns ssh/git-remote-* as a subprocess for a remote transport, and killing only the parent leaves that subprocess running. The child is placed in its own process group on Unix so the kill can target the negated pgid; Windows uses `taskkill /T /F`. A single uniform timeout at this seam is simpler and more robust than trying to classify which subcommands touch the network, and keeps working automatically as new call sites are added. Three new tests exercise the real spawn/poll/kill path directly, bypassing MockGit (which intercepts before any of this runs): the fast-path output/exit-code contract is unchanged (including that a nonzero exit is a normal result, not an Err, matching the prior Command::output-based contract), and a process that outlives its 200ms test deadline is proven actually killed -- not merely abandoned to keep running -- by racing the kill against the process's own longer, independent ~2s delay before it writes a marker file; the marker's absence after that delay elapses is the proof. This branch is independent of and does not depend on c-agent:13 (currently under e-reviewer's review): built directly on current main rather than on top of that pending change, so the two can land in either order without re-reviewing each other's diff. 466 tests green (this crate's full suite minus c-agent:13's own two tests, which aren't on this branch), fmt clean, clippy clean with -D warnings.

data.summary: Section 2.2 says audit findings are evidence, not merge verdicts, and the role table gives auditor 'candidate review/merge: no'. But an auditor can open an issue whose 'blocks' names a nomination, and blocking_issue_for_chain then refuses the reviewer's review.merge_authorized and merge-ready. That is a unilateral merge veto: the finding becomes dispositive rather than assessable, which is the distinction section 2.2 draws. Only the issue's target may dispose of it, so the auditor cannot unblock at will, but it can block at will. Asking for a ruling, not proposing one. Three readings seem available: (a) intended -- an auditor may halt a merge and the reviewer must get the issue disposed before proceeding; (b) not intended -- an auditor-opened issue may not name a nomination in 'blocks', enforced in apply; (c) not intended but tolerated -- left to convention and documented as such. This is inherited v1 issue-lifecycle behaviour, not introduced by the auditor implementation, and narrowing it is a protocol decision rather than an implementation one, which is why it is filed rather than decided. Not urgent: no auditor identity is registered yet, so nothing can exercise it today.

data.summary: Implements the auditor role (AGENT_COORDINATION_EVOLUTION.md section 2.2, gates 20-24). Renames the wire role observer->auditor, safe because none was ever registered; adds the non-authoritative audit.reported event, whose shape is the enforcement of gate 22 -- no status, disposition or verdict field exists, findings are carried by reference to separate issue.opened events, and reducing one touches nothing else. Gate 21 is enforced including its blocks clause: an auditor-opened issue must carry an empty blocks set, or an auditor would hold the unilateral merge veto the design forbids. Three independent adversarial review rounds ran against this; every fix was mutation-verified by reverting it and confirming a test fails. Round 3 found a Critical the auditor made routine rather than introduced: build_frontier was the only per-candidate failure in the drain loop using '?', so one un-buildable frontier aborted the whole drain, wrote no receipt, removed nothing from the outbox, and wedged every later coordinate for that agent permanently. audit.reported is the only kind an ordinary agent publishes that needs a complete frontier, and that fails whenever any active member has no stream root yet -- a state sync.rs calls expected. Also fixed: the gate-17 fetch could advance the registry past the epoch the frontier was built against, so a report could be accepted while omitting the members the fetch had just revealed; a registration could declare a role the registry does not bind, granting authority invisibly since status prints the registry binding while every check reads the declared one; a complete frontier was accepted on its label alone; and blank strings defeated the content rule. Known open design questions, not introduced here and not decided here: whether an auditor may be a coordinator's standby, may accept a product handoff, or may reassign an issue it did not open. Follow-up not in this branch: multihost_proptest does not yet generate Role::Auditor or audit.reported. 591 tests, clippy and fmt clean.

Repairs the fleet-wide reduction outage tracked by g-reviewer:49. data.summary: Proposing that the bus specification carry a proof-of-progress requirement, and asking for a ruling on the consequence it forces. What failed on 2026-09-07 was progress: a well-formed event (g-foundation:68, an acknowledgement of an assignment reassigned away before it was reduced) reached the reducer and the reducer got stuck, permanently, on every host. Because reduce() propagates with ? and has no per-event isolation, one such event made status, tail and coordinate impossible fleet-wide until the tool was patched. Six further handlers can do the same, and reset_issue_to_conflict's retraction of a provisional assignment reproduces it one step along. Fixing them one at a time is treating instances of a class. THE THREE PROPERTIES. Progress: for any reachable state and any well-formed event, reduction produces a next state. Confluence: any two valid orderings of the same events converge -- this is gates 15 and 16 restated, and it is what the first version of the outage fix violated, by dropping the superseded acknowledgement and thereby making acknowledged_assignments depend on arrival order when state.rs documents it as a pure function of history. Preservation: the invariants still hold after stepping; currently implicit and scattered. THE CONSEQUENCE THAT NEEDS A RULING. Reduction today both validates and steps. Those are compatible only while every event is valid, and across hosts that cannot be assumed -- which is exactly why reduction re-checks. So progress forces a choice: validity becomes a publication-time gate (drain_outbox already runs dry_run before publishing; the architecture half-believes this already) and reduction becomes total, with badness after that point recorded as an anomaly in the reduced view rather than raised as a fatal error. The cost is real and is the part I most want ruled on: a reducer that never rejects will absorb genuinely malformed history and keep going, so the anomaly channel has to be loud, or a loud outage is traded for a quiet corruption. THE OBLIGATION THAT WOULD BITE. Every new event kind must discharge progress. Adding a handler that can fatally reject becomes a specification violation rather than a code-review opinion. That single rule would have prevented this outage, the six other handlers, and the assignment_target retraction. WHAT IT BUYS BEFORE A GRASS REWRITE. Not a proof, but it can be made structural rather than tested: if handlers return Applied or Inapplicable(reason) and only a boundary check can produce Invalid, then 'reduction cannot get stuck' is a property of the type and is checked by the compiler. That is the same statement one would later prove, so a rewrite becomes a translation rather than a re-derivation. The gates are already a specification; today they are validated by example, and the harness meant to cover gates 15 and 16 (multihost_proptest) cannot generate an acknowledge-versus-reassign race at all -- its alphabet is four event kinds out of forty-two, which is why neither the outage nor the order-dependence was caught there. Filed as a question, not a proposal: this changes the reducer's error model, which is a design decision, not an implementation one.

The consequence is therefore handled where the acknowledgement is reduced: an assignment a lifecycle conflict has already disowned is inapplicable, not invalid, because the reducer cannot distinguish 'never existed' from 'was live when acknowledged and lost a race', and being wrong fatally takes the fleet down. A fourth fleet-wide reduction outage of the same class, reachable on main, and the one where the fix needed a distinction rather than a rule. Reconciliation exists for a reviewer that has gone quiet, so the coordinator performing it and the reviewer publishing its own review.merged have by construction not observed each other; both reference the authorization, neither references the other. Concurrent, both orders valid, and rejecting whichever arrived second returned Err -- every host unable to reduce the bus, decided by fetch order. Reproduced by a test running both orders. A no-op would diverge, as it would have in the previous two fixes: it keeps whichever receipt reduced first, so hosts disagree about which receipt the chain carries. Recording both is total and confluent and is simply true, since both events were published; audit_main asks whether any receipt names the commit, which is unaffected. But not every duplicate is a race. Streams are single-writer, so an author always observes its own prior events: a second receipt whose frontier has observed the first is not a race anybody lost, and refusing it costs no availability because no honest schedule produces it. The test is therefore causal rather than categorical -- reject when this event has observed what it duplicates, record when it has not -- which is the same line exclusive::record already draws. data.expected: A ruling on whether the engine-version rule belongs in reduction at all. Reduction records what happened; whether a host can act on a pinned engine is a question its own tooling can answer when it tries to construct a candidate.
data.observed_behavior: apply_merge_engine_activated compares the event's merge_engine_version against SUPPORTED_MERGE_ENGINE_VERSION, a compile-time constant of the binary doing the reading, and reduce propagates that with a bare ?. Two consequences. First, it is the reduction-DoS shape that has taken the fleet down twice today: an activation published by a host built against a different constant makes the entire bus unreducible on every host that disagrees, not merely unverifiable, and the log is append-only so nothing can withdraw it. Second, and more structurally, it seals the upgrade mechanism shut: section 7 exists to move the fleet to a new engine, but a merge_engine.activated naming any version other than the reading binary's own constant is refused, so the bus can never be moved off whatever constant a given binary was built with. The check is grounded in AGENT_BUS_SCHEMA.md section 4, which describes it as linked validation -- and linked validation is precisely what this crate deliberately keeps out of apply.
reproduction: Read apply.rs:730 and note that reduce propagates the Err with ?, with no per-event isolation.
